client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the marketing agency about six weeks ago. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one who doesn't have any real experience in marketing, so I constantly feel like I'm falling behind or saying the wrong thing in meetings. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent weight — not in a panicked way, but more like a constant low hum of self-doubt that's been following you into work every day. That feeling of being the "only one" who doesn't have it figured out can be really isolating, even if it's not always loud or dramatic. I'm glad you're here, and I'm curious — when you say everyone else *seems* to know what they're doing, what specifically are you noticing that leads you to that conclusion?

client: I guess it's little things, like when my coworkers speak up in meetings without hesitating, or when they seem to already know the answer before I've even fully understood the question. I sit there trying to look like I'm following along, but inside I'm just hoping no one calls on me. It makes me feel like there's some manual everyone else got that I somehow missed.
therapist: That image of a "missing manual" is really telling — it captures a sense of being on the outside of something everyone else seems to have access to, which can feel quietly exhausting even when nothing dramatic is happening. I want to gently point something out: you're interpreting your coworkers' confidence as evidence that they *know more*, but is it possible that speaking without hesitation and actually having the right answer are two different things? What do you think it would take for you to feel like *you* had that manual — what would need to be true about you or your performance?

client: I mean, yeah, that distinction makes sense in theory — like, confidence isn't the same as competence, I get that. But when I'm sitting in a meeting and someone just rattles off an answer without even pausing to think, it still *feels* like they have something I don't, even if I can't prove it. As for what would need to be true... honestly, I don't even know where that bar is, which is kind of the scariest part.
therapist: That uncertainty about where the bar even *is* — that's often more distressing than simply feeling behind, because there's nothing concrete to work toward or disprove. In CBT terms, we'd call this a moving goalpost, where the standard for "good enough" stays just out of reach no matter what you do, which can quietly keep you stuck. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you six weeks into a new job with no prior experience in that field, what bar would *you* set for them?

client: That's a fair question, and honestly, I'd probably tell a friend that six weeks in, just showing up and learning the basics is enough. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just... doesn't stick. It feels like I'm making an excuse for myself, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily.
therapist: It's really significant that you can see the double standard so clearly — you'd offer a friend genuine compassion, but when you turn that same lens on yourself, it feels like cheating somehow. That belief that self-compassion equals making excuses is actually really common, but it's worth examining — because would you say your friend was "letting themselves off the hook" if they followed your advice, or would you say they were being *realistic*? What do you think that difference reveals about how you're measuring your own worth right now?

client: I guess... if a friend did what I told them to do, I'd say they were being realistic, yeah. But when I think about applying that to myself, there's this voice that says I should just know better, like I don't get the same pass because I'm the one who made the mistake in the first place. It's like I'm holding myself to a completely different standard and I know that's not fair, but knowing it and actually feeling differently about it are two very separate things.
therapist: There's something really important in what you just said — you're not in denial about the double standard, you can see it clearly, and yet the feeling doesn't automatically follow the logic, which is one of the most honest and human things about how our minds work. That voice telling you that you "should just know better" sounds like it carries a lot of history — like it's been around longer than this job. I'm curious, does that voice feel familiar to you from other areas of your life, or does it feel specific to this situation?

client: Yeah, it's... it's definitely not just this job. That voice has been around for as long as I can remember, honestly — like even as a kid I felt like I was supposed to have it all figured out, be the responsible one, not need help. It's exhausting to hear it say the same things now that it said back then, and part of me wonders if it ever actually shuts up or if I just learn to live with it being there.
therapist: There's something both sad and quietly courageous about what you just shared — recognizing that this voice has been a companion since childhood, and still showing up to question it rather than just accepting it as truth. The exhaustion you're describing makes complete sense when you've been carrying that weight for so long. And to answer your question honestly — in my experience, the goal isn't usually to silence that voice forever, but to slowly change your *relationship* with it, so it loses some of its authority over you. I'm wondering, when you think back to that kid who felt like they had to have it all figured out — what was going on around them that made that feel necessary?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... there was a lot of chaos at home, my parents fought constantly and nobody ever seemed to have a handle on anything, so I guess I decided early on that I had to be the one who did. Like if I could just be competent enough, certain enough, maybe things would feel less out of control. It's strange to say out loud because I've never really connected that to why I'm so hard on myself now.
therapist: What you just made is a really profound connection — that the relentless self-criticism wasn't random, it was actually a survival strategy a young child developed to create some sense of safety in an unpredictable world. It makes so much sense that competence became your anchor when everything else felt chaotic, and it's worth holding that with some gentleness, because that kid was doing the best they could with what they had. As you sit with that connection now, what does it feel like to see that critical voice not as a flaw in you, but as something that was once trying to protect you?

client: It's... strange to think about it that way, honestly. Like, part of me wants to accept that framing because it does make a kind of sense, but another part of me feels like it's almost too convenient, like I'm just letting myself off the hook for being so hard on everyone around me too. I guess what I feel is this weird mix of something softening just slightly, and then immediately this guilt that I don't deserve to soften.
therapist: There's something really moving about what you just described — that tiny moment of softening, immediately followed by guilt, as if allowing yourself even a little compassion triggers a kind of alarm. I want to gently name what I'm noticing: you mentioned being hard on people around you too, and it sounds like that guilt might actually be important to explore, not to punish yourself further, but because it seems connected to this same pattern. Can you tell me a little more about what you mean by that — who are you thinking of when you say you've been hard on others?

client: I guess... I'm mostly thinking about my sister. We used to be close, but over the past year or so I've pulled away, and when she does reach out I'm either short with her or I just don't respond at all. And then I feel terrible about it afterward, but instead of fixing it I just... avoid her more, which probably makes her feel like I don't care, when really I care too much and I don't know how to explain any of this to her.
therapist: What you're describing with your sister has a quiet but real ache to it — not explosive, but the kind of hurt that sits in the background and grows heavier the longer it stays unaddressed. It's actually a very recognizable pattern: the more we care about someone, the more exposed and inadequate we can feel around them, so withdrawal becomes a way of protecting both yourself and the relationship from something you're afraid you'll get wrong. I'm curious — when you imagine reaching out to your sister, what's the specific thing you're most afraid she would see in you?

client: I think what I'm most afraid she'd see is that I haven't really figured anything out — like, she has this stable life, her career, her family, and I'm still kind of floundering. It's embarrassing to admit that even to you, because part of me knows she probably wouldn't judge me, but another part of me is convinced that the disappointment would be there even if she never said it out loud. So it's easier to just... stay quiet and keep the distance, even though that distance is its own kind of pain.
therapist: There's a quiet but deep loneliness in what you're describing — holding yourself apart from someone you love, not out of indifference, but out of a fear of being truly seen and found wanting. And I notice you said she "probably wouldn't judge you," which means some part of you already suspects the story you're telling yourself about her disappointment might not be accurate — that it might be *your own* disappointment in yourself that you're projecting onto her. I'm wondering, if your sister could hear everything you've shared with me today — the chaos you grew up in, the way you've been trying to hold it all together since you were a child — do you think she would feel disappointment, or something else entirely?
